Theoretical 2Real exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseEcologyResearchers investigated the effect of the microbiome on the lifespan of the fruit fly (D. melanogaster). To this end, they disinfected fly eggs and transferred them to a sterile food substrate. The non-disinfected eggs served as a control group (“non-axenic”, figure A). Another cohort of the flies (originating from disinfected eggs) was kept on a sterile substrate for the entire lifespan (“axenic”, figures A and B). The rest of the eggs were separated into three groups. They were treated with bacterial cultures either as embryos right after disinfection (figures B, C, D), at day 2 of adulthood (figure D) or at day 7 of adulthood (figure C). The researchers evaluated the fraction of individuals still alive in each population for 100 days, summarizing their results in the graphs below. The percentage in square brackets shows the difference in average lifespan between two populations.
Survival curves (fraction alive vs. days) for axenic, non-axenic, and bacteria-exposed Drosophila populations, exposed to bacteria at different developmental stages.
Using the information and the data in the figures above, determine which of the statements are true or which are false.
A. Exposure to bacteria at the earliest stages of development extends the average lifespan of fruit flies.TRUEFALSEB. Exposure to bacteria at any stage of development can fully restore the lifespan of fruit flies.TRUEFALSEC. The information provided here is sufficient to conclude the possibility that fruit fly lifespan was affected by the egg disinfection technique.TRUEFALSED. The critical period when the presence of bacteria affects the lifespan of fruit flies occurs between day 2 and 7 of adulthood.TRUEFALSECheck AnswersTry Again← Previous: Q82Next: Q84 →Question reproduced from IBO 2022, Theoretical Paper 2, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 - attributed to the International Biology Olympiad. Theoretical 2Real exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseMating Systems & Sexual SelectionResearchers developed two groups of common pigeons, Columba livia, “free choice” and “random union”. In the first group, all the pigeons, both females and males, were released into a single cage, where they were able to freely court and form pairs. In the second, “random union” group, each of multiple cages was filled with one male and one female together, until they began to court and form pairs, after which the pairs were released into a common cage. In the “free choice” group, the courtship process took significantly longer than in the “random union” group. However, the pairs of the “free choice” group started to breed earlier and laid more fertilized eggs. In both groups, the attractiveness of different individuals for the opposite sex (both males and females) was very different. In the “free choice” group, the couples formed from individuals with similar levels of attractiveness (both partners had high, medium or low attractiveness), while in the “random union” group this pairing pattern was not present.
Using the information above, determine which of the statements are true or which are false.
A. The only explanation for the pairing pattern observed in the "free-choice" group is that the birds were aiming to pair with a similarly attractive individual.TRUEFALSEB. The reproductive rate in the "random union" group of common pigeons is due to the possibility of forming pairs of males and females of the matching level of attractiveness.TRUEFALSEC. The freedom to choose a partner increases the reproductive capacity of common pigeons.TRUEFALSED. Results of this experiment suggest that over time the population of common pigeon will be selected for more attractive traits.TRUEFALSECheck AnswersTry Again← Previous: Q87Next: Q89 →Question reproduced from IBO 2022, Theoretical Paper 2, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 - attributed to the International Biology Olympiad. data:
Theoretical 2Real exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseMating Systems & Sexual SelectionDuring the breeding season, Notophthalmus viridescens newts form groups. A mature female produces pheromones, and has a full abdomen of eggs and actively seeks a mate. Males also secrete pheromones, exhibit coloured spots, display courtship behavior in the form of wiggling movements, and compete specifically for larger females. During amplexus, the male clasps the female’s body with his hind limbs for up to three hours (Figure 1), during which time he exhibits various behaviors, such as cheek rubbing, tail vibration and forelimb rubbing. Rival males could occasionally try to dislodge the mating male during amplexus. Following amplexus, the male deposits his sperm packet on the bottom of the pond. Females use their cloacas to collect the sperm packets. Rival males can also release sperm packets close to the mating pair and these could be collected by the female as well. Fertilized eggs are laid over the following few weeks.
Figure 1. Amplexus of Notophthalmus viridescens newts: the male is on top.
Using the information above, determine which of the statements are true or which are false.
A. Male-male contests can occur both through the competition over larger-bodied females and during amplexus.TRUEFALSEB. A male uses both olfactory and tactile cues to both attract the female and also stimulate her during amplexus.TRUEFALSEC. Females actively seek larger-bodied males to ensure their own reproductive success.TRUEFALSED. There are apparently no mechanisms for sperm competition to occur in this newt species.TRUEFALSECheck AnswersTry Again← Previous: Q88Next: Q90 →Question reproduced from IBO 2022, Theoretical Paper 2, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 - attributed to the International Biology Olympiad. data:
Theoretical 2Real exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseForaging & Anti-Predator BehaviorThe South American (French Guiana) cane toad (Rhinella marina) was introduced to Australia about 90 years ago to control the cane beetle (Dermolepida albohirtum) populations. To study the adaptive features of the species under the new conditions, the phenomena of cannibalism and the duration of the early larval stage (non-feeding) were studied.
In the first experiment, the late-stage tadpoles of native South American and invasive Australian populations were released into two separate aquariums, each divided by a maze. One part of each aquarium contained clean water and the other part had newly hatched larvae of the same source population (Figures A, B). In the second experiment, tadpoles and larvae of the respective populations were placed together in two separate aquaria and the proportion of cannibalism was recorded for each population (Figure C). In the third experiment, to study the duration of the early larval stage (non-feeding), the larvae of each population were divided into two groups. One was kept in clean water and the other in an aquarium containing late-stage tadpoles of the same population (Figure D).
Figure: A, B - Graphs of movement of tadpoles in the aquarium (A – South American, B – Australian). Horizontal axis – time, vertical axis – the proportion of tadpoles. White circles – tadpoles swimming towards clean water, black circles – tadpoles swimming towards larvae. C - the proportion of larvae cannibalized; D - duration of the pre-feeding stages determined in separate aquariums, one with clean water (control), the other with late-stage larvae (experimental). Solid lines: p < 0.05.
Using the information and the figures above, determine which of the statements are true or which are false.
A. South American tadpoles prefer clean water.TRUEFALSEB. Cannibalism has been reported more frequently in the Australian toad population than in the South American population, becoming a stable form of feeding behavior.TRUEFALSEC. In the Australian population, the early larval stage has been significantly reduced in duration, which can be seen as an adaptation to avoid cannibalism.TRUEFALSED. A decrease in the duration of the early larval stage was observed in the experimental groups of both South American and Australian toads.TRUEFALSECheck AnswersTry Again← Previous: Q89Next: Q91 →Question reproduced from IBO 2022, Theoretical Paper 2, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 - attributed to the International Biology Olympiad. Theoretical 2Real exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseAnimal CommunicationResearchers noted that males of small tree finches (Camarhynchus parvulus) sing by repeating one specific syllable over and over. They also found that 4 unique syllables occur among males collected from Santa Cruz island, 3 unique syllables occur among males from Floreana island, and 3 additional syllables are common among both. To make quantitative measurements, they decided to summarize the behavioral activity of every individual in response to a song by a numerical score (behavioral activity scores are on the Y-axis in the plots below). In the first experiment, researchers subjected an individual from each population to a song recording from its native or foreign island. In the second experiment, they subjected each individual to a song recording containing its own syllable (homotypic) or a different syllable (heterotypic).
(1) Geographic origin of the intruder song and (2) syllable type of the intruder song: behavioral response scores for Santa Cruz and Floreana finches. Asterisks denote a statistically significant difference.
Using the information and the figures above, determine whether the following statements are true or false.
A. Male finches can recognize intruders from another population by their song.TRUEFALSEB. Male finches change their behavior significantly when they hear a song with unfamiliar syllables.TRUEFALSEC. The first figure shows that male finches acquire their defining syllables genetically.TRUEFALSED. The second figure shows that the presence of common syllables between Santa Cruz and Floreana populations is a result of evolutionary convergence.TRUEFALSECheck AnswersTry Again← Previous: Q90Next: Q92 →Question reproduced from IBO 2022, Theoretical Paper 2, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 - attributed to the International Biology Olympiad. data:
Theoretical 2Real exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseAggression, Territoriality & Social StructureIn their seminal paper from 1973, J.M. Smith and G.R. Price used computer modeling to investigate intraspecific animal interactions. They assumed two mechanisms by which animals can inflict damage: soft, also known as “conventional” (e.g. snakes wrestling) and hard, also known as “dangerous” (e.g. snakes biting each other). They assigned positive rewards for the early retreat (accounting for saved resources) or winning (accounting for obtained resources) and negative rewards for receiving damage. Simulations were performed for various matches of stereotyped behaviors (“Mouse”, “Hawk”, “Bully”, “Retaliator”, and “Prober-Retaliator”). Averages of final rewards for each match are summarized below, with more positive values indicative of a more favorable outcome for the individual with that behavior type. For example, a “Bully” gets 80.0 points in a match against a “Mouse”, while the “Mouse” gets 19.5 points in a match against the “Bully”.
Focal strategy ↓ vs. opponent → “Mouse” “Hawk” “Bully” “Retaliator” “Prober-Retaliator” “Mouse” 29.0 19.5 19.5 29.0 17.2 “Hawk” 80 -19.5 74.6 -18.1 -18.9 “Bully” 80 4.9 41.5 11.9 11.2 “Retaliator” 29.0 -22.3 57.1 29.0 23.1 “Prober-Retaliator” 56.7 -20.1 59.4 26.9 21.9 Table: average payoff to the row (focal) strategy in a match against the column (opponent) strategy.
Assuming that in a mixed population, all fights occur between randomly chosen pairs, determine whether the following statements are true or false.
A. In a population with 90% "hawks" and 10% of "mice", "mice" would eventually go extinct.TRUEFALSEB. data:
Theoretical 2Real exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseImmune PhysiologyIdentifying new applications for approved drugs outside of the scope of their original medical indication is an important strategy in modern pharmaceutics. This strategy is often based on transcriptome analysis. It is assumed that upon administration, the drug causes significant changes in the expression of a particular gene set or sets. These changes characterize the effect of the drug. If the targeted gene set is also associated with a disease (e.g., the gene set is overexpressed during the disease and underexpressed upon drug administration), the studied drug may be a candidate for the disease treatment.
The drug Infliximab’s effect on Crohn’s disease (CD), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), sarcoidosis and ulcerative colitis (UC) has been studied using the transcriptome-based approach. Infliximab is an immunosuppressive agent used to treat CD and UC. Gene expression data was obtained from the colonic biopsy samples of CD patients, Infliximab- or placebo-treated UC patients, as well as from lung tissue of COPD and sarcoidosis patients. The results of the analysis are summarized in Figure 1 below. Figure 1A shows the summary heatmap of the transcriptome. Gene sets with the same expression patterns form spots on the heatmap (A, D, etc.). Colors red to blue (from warm to cold) indicate the expression level from upregulation (overexpressed) to downregulation (underexpressed), correspondingly. Figure 1B shows the expression of spots (A, D, etc.) in the test specimens relative to the control (healthy, placebo, or before Infliximab administration). Figure 1C shows quantitative analysis of spot expression profiles.
Figure 1. Evaluation of Infliximab’s effect on UC, CD, COPD, and sarcoidosis. (A) Global transcriptome summary heatmap with identified potentially therapeutically relevant gene clusters - spots (A, D, F, T, U, V, X). (B) Drug- and disease-spot perturbation heatmap. (C) Quantitative analysis of spot expression profiles.
Based on these results, determine whether the following statements are true or false.
A. Spot U's expression, which was upregulated in UC, CD, and sarcoidosis, can be antagonistically targeted by Infliximab.TRUEFALSEB. Spot F, which was upregulated in UC, is associated with response to infliximab.TRUEFALSEC. Expression perturbation in each of the studied spots is associated with at least one disease from the experiment.TRUEFALSED. UC is characterized by downregulation of spots A and D.TRUEFALSECheck AnswersTry Again← Previous: Q95Next: Q97 →Question reproduced from IBO 2022, Theoretical Paper 2, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 - attributed to the International Biology Olympiad. data:
Theoretical 2Real exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseDNA Structure & ReplicationThere are two mechanisms of telomere lengthening in a cell: the telomerase-dependent (TEL) pathway and the alternative telomere-lengthening (ALT) pathway. The activity of the TEL and ALT pathways has been studied in a number of healthy human tissues based on the expression of the genes involved in those pathways (see Figure). A pathway is considered active if the relative activity value is greater than 0.
Gene effect is measured by the Partial Influence (PI) metric. If PI is greater than 0, the gene activates the pathway; if less than 0, it suppresses the pathway; if 0, it does not affect the pathway activity. The greater the absolute value of PI, the greater the effect of that gene on pathway activation. Relative expression is the natural logarithm of the expression of a gene in a sample divided by the mean of the expression of that gene in all samples.
Figure (panels C–E). The relative activity values of the TEL and ALT pathways in testis across age groups (C–D), and a TMM scatter plot for testis (E).
Figure (panels F–G). Gene influence on TEL and ALT pathway activity in testis, measured by Partial Influence (PI).
Using this information and analysis, determine whether the following statements are true or false.
A. RAD51 is the most critical factor resulting in activation of the ALT in testis.TRUEFALSEB. TERC decreases the activation of the TEL pathway in testisTRUEFALSEC. The relative activity values of the TEL pathway are clearly divided into two age groupsTRUEFALSED. TEL pathway activity predominates at a younger age, while the ALT pathway is more important in older ageTRUEFALSECheck AnswersTry Again← Previous: Q96Next: Q98 →Question reproduced from IBO 2022, Theoretical Paper 2, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 - attributed to the International Biology Olympiad. data:
Theoretical 2Real exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseGenetic Drift, Gene Flow & MutationThe evolution of grape species is closely connected to the historical and cultural development of humans. Archaeological research shows that the cultivation of grapes began 8000–10000 years ago in the Middle East and South Caucasus. To understand the genetic diversity and evolution of grapes, single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) of about 800 cultivars have been studied. As a result, a genomic map for each cultivar was obtained, and the distribution of point mutations indicated on them (Figure). The closer the mutations are located to each other on the map, the more likely they are to be found together in a genome. The red “mountains” on the map indicate a high probability of mutations in that area, and the blue “plains” a low probability. The summary map shows the variety of mutations found across cultivars. The map is annotated with the names of geographical areas found to be associated with the mutation groups. Further phylogenetic analysis of cultivars revealed two geographical routes of crop evolution: northern (from the Caucasus to the Balkans to Western Europe) and southern (through Palestine, Maghreb to the Iberian Peninsula). These paths are shown with arrows on the map.
Figure. Genomic maps of grape cultivars: individual cultivar SNP-landscapes and an overview landscape annotated with geographic regions and the two proposed migration routes of cultivated grapes.
Based on the results, indicate whether the following statements are true or false.
A. The results support the archaeological theory that the cultivation of grapes began in the South Caucasus (Georgia, Armenia) and Barber Mahik (Eastern Anatolia, Northern Lebanon and Syria).TRUEFALSEB. The main reason for dichotomous branching in the evolution of grape cultivars is the Mediterranean Sea, which is the biggest barrier to genetic exchange.TRUEFALSEC. The Pyrenees is a greater barrier for plant genetic exchange than the Strait of Gibraltar.TRUEFALSED. Genetic differences in Spanish Mencia and French Mireille cultivars can be explained by sympatric speciation.TRUEFALSECheck AnswersTry Again← Previous: Q97Next: Q99 →Question reproduced from IBO 2022, Theoretical Paper 2, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 - attributed to the International Biology Olympiad. Around 100 years ago, the small white hare Lepus americanus (up to 52 cm in length and up to 1.55 kg) was introduced to the island. Lepus arcticus currently inhabits only open areas and Lepus americanus inhabits only forested areas. The forested areas are also inhabited by a predator of hares - the Canada lynx Lynx canadensis.

Theoretical AReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licensePhylogenetic Trees & CladisticsKazakhstan boasts a rich ecosystem harboring numerous species of tulips, some of which are direct ancestors to many modern cultivated varieties. It’s worth noting that T. borszczowii has the same features as the common ancestor among these tulip species.

Theoretical AReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseCell Theory, Prokaryotes & EukaryotesMagnetotactic bacteria have magnetosomes (magnetite crystals with a lipid membrane) arranged in a line, helping them find water with suitable oxygen levels in the oxic-anoxic transition zone (OATZ in Figure 1B). These bacteria are classified into two types: polar, which align their body orientation with the magnetic field, and axial, which can have two orientations along the magnetic field axis. In the Earth’s Northern and Southern hemispheres, polar bacteria magnetosomes have opposite polarities. To stay in the OATZ, polar bacteria change the rotation direction of their flagella based on oxygen concentration.
Figure 1. A Magnetotactic bacteria with labeled magnetosomes, the lower image shows the magnetic field generated. B Northern hemisphere polar bacteria in water, OATZ - suitable oxygen level. C Experimental setup: water-filled tube with two openings in a magnetic field. Bacteria start in the anoxic zone (red).

Axial magnetotactic bacteria will form 2 distinct bands in experimental setup.TRUEFALSED. Polar magnetotactic bacteria from the southern hemisphere will start a counterclockwise rotation of flagella when placed into experimental setup.TRUEFALSECheck AnswersTry Again← Previous: Q9Next: Q11 →Question reproduced from IBO 2024, Theoretical Exam Part A, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 - attributed to the International Biology Olympiad. Theoretical AReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseRecombinant DNA & Biotechnology TechniquesDirected evolution is a process that mimics natural selection by artificially applying selective pressure to organisms to screen and select for a desired phenotype. Directed evolution can be employed in protein engineering.
The Escherichia coli AL strain was engineered by deleting specific pathways that regenerate NAD⁺ (Figure 1). NAD⁺ regeneration can be restored by introducing a foreign enzyme, referred to as Enzyme D, which converts an exogenous substrate, not naturally connected to the native metabolic network, into a non-toxic product using NADH as a cofactor. A library comprising randomized mutants of Enzyme D is introduced into the engineered E. coli AL strain.
Figure 1. A: exogenous substrate present in large intestine; B: library variants of enzyme D; C: carbon source; D: enzyme D.

Medical personnel noticed a garlic-like odor, typically caused by sulfur-containing substances, emanating from her mouth, and white crystals formed in a blood sample taken from her. Subsequently, the medical staff began losing consciousness and having convulsions.
This 1994 incident at Riverside General Hospital was initially thought to be mass hysteria, later suspicion fell on DMSO₄: prior to admission, the patient had applied excessive amounts of DMSO-based ointments for analgesic purposes. While DMSO itself is non-toxic to humans, DMSO₄ is classified as a warfare agent. It rapidly undergoes the following reaction:
$$DMSO_4 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 2CH_3OH + H_2SO_4 \quad (1)$$

Species richness is lowest at the poles and highest on the equator. The ubiquity of this pattern suggests the possibility of a single general explanation but our understanding of this pattern is incomplete. The current latitudinal zones arose approximately 45 million years ago, after a period in which the Earth was primarily tropical. The following three hypotheses (Figure 1A-C) could possibly explain this gradient:
Figure 1. A difference in carrying capacity. B difference in diversification rate. C difference in the starting point of diversification. Note that in each graph only one factor is changed.

Figure 1. Walker Circulation.
Alterations in Walker Circulation are called El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO). This oscillation has 3 phases: Neutral (normal Walker Circulation), El Niño (weak or reversed Walker Circulation), and La Niña (strong Walker Circulation). Here are some examples of the influence of ENSO on smaller ecosystems:
Figure 2. Top left: Global context of the smaller ecosystems mentioned. A, B, and C represent data from the corresponding ecosystems.

Theoretical AReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseEcologyFractal geometry can be illustrated by Mandelbrot’s question: How long is the coast of Britain? The answer depends on the scale of measurement.
Analogously, ecosystems exhibit scale-dependent resource availability. For instance, measuring Admiralty Island’s coastline from the perspective of an eagle (using the distance between nests) yields 761 km, whereas considering barnacles (requiring 2 cm of space) results in 11,000 km.
Figure 1B shows the relationship between the coastline length of Admiralty Island and the scale at which it is measured, as defined by the equation on the graph. A similar relationship exists for the amount of resources available for a species that operates at a given scale, as well as for its biomass.
Figure 1. A Admiralty island. B Log-log graph of resolution (scale) and the length of Admiralty coastline; a, b - species; Q - resource available or biomass or coastline length, k - constant, L - scale, d - fractal dimension describing the complexity of the pattern, more complex patterns correspond to higher values of d.

While they eventually will be restored, this happens on a geological timescale. Less than 1% of total water is available for human use - renewable freshwater resources (RFWR) - and even from this small fraction of water, only 10% is enough to fulfill the needs of humanity. While theoretically, there is more than enough water, many regions still experience a water crisis - a lack of accessible RFWR or an inability to utilize available RFWR.

Theoretical AReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseMechanisms of BehaviorRoads are responsible for habitat fragmentation, impeding wildlife movement via the “Barrier effect,” which combines direct mortality from collisions with animal avoidance behaviour. Note that animal response to moving cars can resemble their reaction to natural danger stimuli. The research identified four types of animal behavioural responses (see Table 1) based on their perceived danger from traffic. Each animal species typically exhibits only one of these behavioral responses.
Behavior type Description Speeders Their primary response to threats is to flee across the road. Avoiders Avoid the road at much lower traffic volume and remain further from the road than other types. Nonresponders Do not cease their movement at any level of traffic intensity. Pausers Reduce their speed by freezing, which increases the time spent on the roadway. Table 1. Types of animal behavioural responses to traffic. Traffic volume entails the number of vehicles passing a point on a road segment.
Figure 1. The total barrier effect (B, black solid line) from mortality (M, blue dashed line) and avoidance (A, red dotted line) for the four response categories. X - traffic volume in arbitrary units. Y - magnitude of the barrier effect in term probability (from 0 to 1).

Theoretical AReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseDevelopment & LearningIndividual progress and subsequent social learning are important aspects of group living. The progressive accumulation of culture within a group over time is called Cumulative Cultural Evolution (CCE). The following study aimed to investigate the interplay between CCE and collective decision-making. Theoretical AReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseMendel's Laws & Probability in GeneticsImagine a planet inhabited by animal-like creatures capable of both meiosis and mitosis, where the fundamental principles of genetics apply. This species is distinguished by two alternating heteromorphic generations: haploid and diploid.
The haploid (n) generation consists of intelligent beings who dwell in urban environments and form pairs of sexual partners. In contrast, individuals of the diploid (2n) generation are non-rational and aggressive and are reared in specialized nurseries. The haploid pairs entrust their offspring to these nurseries, where the diploid organisms give rise to a new haploid generation.
In one locus of these organisms, there are three alleles: A1 (most dominant) > A2 > A3 (most recessive). Among the 2n generation, 1% of organisms have the A3 phenotype, 8% have the A2 phenotype, and 91% have the A1 phenotype. The entire population is in genetic equilibrium.

data:
Theoretical AReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseMacroevolutionary Patterns & Mass ExtinctionsMass extinctions occur when environmental changes outpace rates of species adaptation. One way to quantify this change is by measuring the addition of inorganic carbon to oceans over time. Significant changes in the flux between inorganic and organic carbon reservoirs are termed carbon cycle perturbation events. Mass change measures the magnitude of change in inorganic carbon mass in oceans. Another quantifying metric of a carbon cycle, isotopic shift measures the change in carbon isotopic composition during the event.
In the last 220 million years, the biological pump, which transports organic carbon and calcium carbonate from the ocean’s surface to the deep sea, has significantly strengthened.

The frequency with which a particular mutation appears de novo is described by the fundamental property of each species - distribution of fitness effects (DFE). There are two direct methods of finding DFE: induce mutations and check the fitness of each mutation, or prepare mutation accumulation lines and compare their fitness distribution with the initial line. DFE can also be inferred indirectly from sequencing data that compares rates of non-synonymous (N) and synonymous (S) substitutions using the dN/dS ratio between different species.

Theoretical AReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseCalvin Cycle, Photorespiration & C4/CAM BiochemistryDuring the Calvin Cycle, carbon dioxide is fixed by RuBisCo, an enzyme in plants. However, RuBisCo can also catalyze reactions with oxygen, which disrupts the photosynthesis.
Photorespiration is a process of recovering ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP, the RuBisCo substrate) from products of RuBisCo oxygenation. Recent studies suggest it plays a significant role in NADH generation, managing the metabolic toxin 2-phosphoglycolate (2-PG), and connecting photosynthesis to nutrient assimilation and abiotic stress response pathways.
Figure 1. A schematic of photorespiration. When overexpressed, the enzyme in dark green (square) increases the rate of reactions, the enzyme in orange (stars) does not affect it, and the enzyme in magenta (circle) slows it down. Theoretical AReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseStomatal Physiology & Gas ExchangePoaceae (grass family) stomata have a “dumbbell” shape and a stronger connection between guard and subsidiary cells. Due to this adaptation, they respond to stimuli faster than non-Poaceae stomata. Specifically, alternating hyperpolarization (H) and depolarization (D) of cell membranes allow well-synced osmotic flow by activating the ion channels, as shown in Figure 1. Non-Poaceae stomata do not sync this closely.
Due to the advanced geometry of Poaceae stomata, subsidiary cells actually lose turgor when guard cells gain it, and vice versa. That leads to the widest possible open pore, as the subsidiary cell “bends inward” to accommodate the growing guard cell.
Figure 1. A) Schematic representation of Poaceae stomata synchronization mechanism. Guard cells are GC, and subsidiary cells are SC on the diagram. Question marks imply the effect has only partially been verified; blue H2O cylinders are aquaporins. B) Highlighted micrograph of a Poaceae (i) and non-Poaceae (ii) stomata.

Theoretical AReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseLight Reactions & PhotophosphorylationXanthophylls are yellow-orange colored and fat-soluble photoprotective pigments. This is likely an adaptation to the unforgiving sunlight in dry ecosystems. As excess light leads to the accumulation of protons in the thylakoid’s lumen, this lower pH triggers a transformation of precursors (Pre-Z) into zeaxanthin (Z). All of them are xanthophylls.
When protonated, Z changes the conformation of photosystem II to dissipate extra light energy as heat. Reduced ascorbate is a cofactor for de-epoxidase, the enzyme that catalyzes the Pre-Z → Z reactions.

Theoretical AReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseWater Transport & TranspirationFluid dynamics put an upper limit on how high a tree’s water column might exist, and above that limit, water transport in the xylem will be disrupted. However, trees similar to Californian redwoods routinely grow above this limit. Scientists studied Californian Sequoia sempervirens from the alluvial flood plain and Sequoiadendron giganteum from the mountain slopes with most likely dry soil. Xylem adaptations have higher water and carbon cost upfront than stomatal adaptations, but allow plants to transpire more.
Figure 1. Plots like the one above condense many variables like leaf conductance and wood density into two categories. Low PC2 values correspond to more efficient stomatal water use, and high PC2 to more efficient xylem water use. PC3 values are inversely proportional to leaf mass and wood density. The bigger the symbol, the taller is that particular tree. Middle-size symbols are a different shape to make telling apart easier.

Despite that, Rubisco only uses CO2 as the carbon source.
The oceanic pH is around 8, and freshwater pH is around 7. Generally for aquatic plants, epidermal cells take up carbon directly, but diffusion is significantly slower in water than in air. Plants can uptake HCO3- faster than CO2. Some plants use intracellular carbonic anhydrase as a quicker carbon sourcing mechanism.

Theoretical AReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseForaging & Anti-Predator BehaviorElectric eels (Electrophorus electricus) are predatory fish that utilize electrical and mechanical signals during hunting. They emit two types of electrical impulses: low-voltage, which induces sudden muscle contraction of the prey, and high-voltage, which paralyzes the prey, aiding in capture and consumption.
In the experiment conducted for studying electrolocation mechanisms of eels, a container with two compartments was used, as shown in Figure 1. The lower compartment contained an isolated fresh fish corpse attached to electrodes, connecting it to the upper compartment’s environment. Additionally, several electrically non-conductive rods and one conductive rod were placed beneath the transparent, perforated divider.
Results of the experiment indicated that upon placement in the container, the eel began attacking the conductive rod, but not the fish corpse (Figure 2). Assume that the fish corpse was supplied with a sufficient amount of ATP.
Figure 1. Experiment setup; black arrow - conductive rod.
Figure 2. A Impulses recorded from the upper compartment (x-axis - time, y-axis - voltage); LW - low voltage impulse, HW - high voltage impulse. Theoretical AReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseCardiovascular PhysiologyEsophageal Doppler Monitoring (EDM) is a minimally invasive method to measure blood flow in the aorta and assess cardiac output. A Doppler probe is inserted into the esophagus near the aorta. The principle behind the measurement is the detection of changes in frequency (Doppler shift) of ultrasound waves reflected by moving red blood cells. Using the Doppler effect, the probe calculates blood flow velocity from the equation Δf = 2vf₀cos(θ)/cₛ, where cos(θ) = √2/2, cₛ = 1540 m/s, and f₀ = 4 MHz.
The resulting waveform provides important data on heart function, such as stroke volume and cardiac output, which helps guide clinical decisions in real-time.
Figure 1. A Placement of the Doppler probe in the esophagus near the aorta to measure blood flow velocity (red arrow). B Doppler waveform showing linear blood velocity (cm/s) over time (s), with a peak systolic velocity of 100 cm/s. The area under the curve shows the distance traveled by blood.
On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

After the antibody binds to the antigen (in our case, glycoside), the enzyme linked to the antibody catalyzes the added substrate, leading to a color change that can be measured by spectrophotometry at 405 nm. The following heatmaps represent the ELISA results based on the position of change and the amino acid to which wild-type amino acid was mutated.
Figure 1. A Binding data of antibodies mutated in the positions described in the figure to the four glycosides. The absorbance, which correlates to the binding strength of digoxigenin (P), ouabain (Q), digoxin (R), and digitoxin (S) to the mutated antibodies, was linearly scaled to that of the wild-type (labeled in red) which was assigned a value of 1.0 (labels of glycosides P, Q, R, and S should not be confused with the one-letter codes of amino acids). Theoretical AReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseComparative Osmoregulation & ExcretionThe countercurrent system is a common biological pattern, classified into countercurrent multipliers and exchangers. In vertebrates, these systems often involve a specialized network of arteries and veins lying close together, known as the rete mirabile. In humans, an example of this system is found in the kidneys, where the nephron and vasa recta together form a countercurrent multiplier. This arrangement allows for efficient exchange and concentration of solutes and water, which are crucial in urine concentration and maintaining the body’s fluid balance.
Figure 1. A Countercurrent osmotic multiplier: solute passes through a reservoir separated by a semipermeable membrane; black arrows show water movement driven by pressure P. B Nephron diagram: 1 - descending limb, 2 - ascending limb, 3 - collecting duct. Numbers indicate osmolarity (mOsmol/kg).

Theoretical AReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseProtein Structure, Folding & FunctionThe bonds between the central carbon atom and attached groups in peptides can rotate freely. The rotation angles of the N-Cα and Cα-C bonds are called φ (phi) and ψ (psi) angles, respectively. To measure the φ angle, first draw the Cα-C bond horizontally so that the N group is at 0 degrees (in the same plane as the Cα-C bond). Then rotate the distal N group around the Cα-C bond until the structure matches the structure that you aim to measure as shown in Figure 1C. For the ψ angle, place the N-Cα bond horizontally and rotate the distal C group. The Ramachandran plot visually represents the combinations of φ and ψ angles in a peptide backbone (Figure 1B).
Figure 1. A Part of the peptide with shown φ and ψ angles. B The Ramachandran plot with the values of φ and ψ angles for all the amino acid residues except Gly in the rabbit’s pyruvate kinase. C The φ angle values are created by the rotation. D Three structures of amino acids’ residues.

Theoretical AReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseGene Regulation: Eukaryotic & EpigeneticsCertain loci in the genome are influenced by epigenetic modifications, but understanding their precise mechanisms remains challenging. The IGF2-H19 locus serves as a well-known example, regulated by the methylation state of the imprinting control region (ICR). The donor (D) can be excited by light of a specific wavelength, raising the energy of an electron in the molecule. When far away from the acceptor (A), it will emit light via fluorescence. However, when it is within 10 nm of an acceptor molecule, it can “transfer” its energy to the acceptor, which then releases the absorbed energy as a different wavelength of light.
For an efficient FRET, the emission spectra of the donor must overlap with the excitation spectra of the acceptor. Theoretical BReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseEcologyThe Lotka-Volterra model is used to predict the dynamics of competing populations. It is based on the following equations and is analyzed by constructing specific lines:
$$\frac{dN_1}{dt} = r_1 N_1 \left(\frac{K_1 - N_1 - \alpha N_2}{K_1}\right), \qquad \frac{dN_2}{dt} = r_2 N_2 \left(\frac{K_2 - N_2 - \beta N_1}{K_2}\right)$$
where K - carrying capacity, N - number of individuals, r - intrinsic rate of increase, α - competition coefficient of species 2 on species 1, β - competition coefficient of species 1 on species 2, and dN/dt = population growth rate.
The Lotka-Volterra line represents the number of individuals in a population at equilibrium (dN/dt = 0). For two species in competition, there are only 4 combinations of the location of these lines. Depending on the initial values of populations, the future changes in populations’ dynamics can be predicted.
Figure 1. A Lotka-Volterra lines. B Combinations of line locations and trends - arrows show the further direction of populations’ dynamics for particular initial values, indicated by blue dots.
On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.
A. The y-intercept for line of species 1 is equal to K1/α.TRUEFALSEB. This model takes into account the presence of intraspecific competition.TRUEFALSEC. Suppose that there is a certain community of elks (K1 = 200, α = 1) and deer (K2 = 100, β = 2) competing with each other. If the current populations are 120 elks and 60 deer, the elks will eventually outcompete the deer.TRUEFALSED. In only 2 scenarios out of 4 described in Figure 1B both species can stably coexist.TRUEFALSECheck AnswersTry Again← Previous: Q14Next: Q16 →Question reproduced from IBO 2024, Theoretical Exam Part B, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 - attributed to the International Biology Olympiad. The balance of limiting factors creates trade-offs, allowing more than one species to occupy different “dimensions” within a niche; otherwise, a more adapted species will completely displace a less adapted one.
In the steppe conditions, Stipa capillata is more resistant to drought compared to other perennial grasses. However, since its root system is weak, it cannot spread vigorously in grasslands with good perennial turf.
Turf is a surface layer of soil, densely overgrown with short herbaceous plants very close to the ground.
Figure 1. Stipa capillata.

data:
Theoretical BReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseExtranuclear & Non-Mendelian InheritanceGenomic imprinting is one mechanism by which sexes can encourage favourable traits in a fetus to maximize their own reproductive success. The most evident imprinting phenomenon occurs when the normal gene expression is disrupted.
Particularly, Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome (BWS) is characterized by fetal macrosomia (birth weight >90th percentile) and an increased risk of congenital tumors. Meanwhile, babies with Silver–Russell syndrome (SRS) are born small for their gestational age and later exhibit dwarfism.
Both cases can be associated with genetic defects in clusters of imprinted genes on chromosome 11. IGF2 is a pro-proliferative regulator of fetal growth. H19 knockout does not have pathological consequences. Another paternally imprinted gene (active on a maternal chromosome) is IGF2R; its protein binds IGF2 and targets it for lysosomal degradation.
Figure 1. Maternal and Paternal structures of the IGF2-H19 cluster. ICR - imprinting control region; En - Enhancer, Met - methylated, unMet - unmethylated.

Individuals with the maternal IGF2R loss of function will have the phenotype resembling that of the BWS patients.TRUEFALSED. When Channel A opens, it allows an influx of calcium ions (Ca²⁺) into the cytosol. This rise in cytosolic Ca²⁺ triggers further calcium release from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) via ryanodine and inositol trisphosphate receptors, and can activate Channel B to sustain the calcium signal. Mitochondria help modulate this calcium signaling by buffering excess Ca²⁺, which influences both energy production and cellular responses.
In mitochondria, calcium activates Krebs cycle enzymes (isocitrate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase), enhancing ATP production. Also, in these cells, calcium release triggers insulin release in response to high glucose levels.

Table 1 shows pharmacokinetic properties that regulate the duration of a drug’s therapeutic effect.
Property Description Absorption - Distribution Influenced by ionization and other biochemical properties of the compound, as well as polarity, transport-protein binding, and blood flow. The volume of distribution (V) describes a drug’s ability to disperse within body fluids - a V close to the total body volume indicates the best distribution. Metabolism Primarily occurs in the liver. First-pass metabolism happens when the liver metabolizes a drug before it enters systemic circulation. A drug’s half-life is the time for its blood concentration to halve. A prodrug is a drug that becomes active only after being metabolized (typically in the liver). Excretion Kidneys typically eliminate hydrophilic substances, while hydrophobic ones exit via bile. Only about 5% of bile salts (and drugs) are excreted; the rest is reabsorbed, transported to the liver, and re-secreted with bile - known as enterohepatic circulation. Table 1. data:
Theoretical BReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseCardiovascular PhysiologyHuman bodies have different types of capillaries that differ in wall structure, depending on the function of the organ they are located in.
Oncotic pressure is a pressure driven by proteins in the solution.
Below is the Starling equation, which governs the fluid exchange across capillaries:
$$J_v = K_f\left((P_c - P_i) - \sigma(\pi_c - \pi_i)\right) \qquad (1)$$
where,
Symbol Meaning $K_f$ filtration coefficient $P_c$ capillary hydrodynamic pressure $P_i$ interstitial hydrodynamic pressure $\pi_c$ capillary oncotic pressure $\pi_i$ interstitial oncotic pressure $\sigma$ reflection coefficient When Jv is positive, there is a net fluid movement out of the capillary (filtration); when Jv is negative, there is a net fluid movement into the capillary (absorption).
In a simple model, Pc is influenced by arterial and venous pressures, and can be summarized by the following formula:
$$P_c = \frac{0.2 P_a + P_v}{1.2} \qquad (2)$$
where Pa and Pv are arterial and venous pressures, respectively.
On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.
A. In a person with a very low protein content in their diet for a long period of time, the filtration level tends to be increased.TRUEFALSEB. Capillary wall integrity might directly affect the Kf value.TRUEFALSEC. Venous constriction has a more pronounced effect on Pc value than arterial constriction.TRUEFALSED. Fluid exchange between capillaries and plasma protein-synthesizing liver cells is governed mainly by hydrodynamic pressures rather than oncotic pressures.TRUEFALSECheck AnswersTry Again← Previous: Q41Next: Q43 →Question reproduced from IBO 2024, Theoretical Exam Part B, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 - attributed to the International Biology Olympiad. Theoretical BReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseRespiratory PhysiologyLung volumes can change in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD). Figure 1 summarizes normal lung volumes and the changes that occur at different stages of COPD. Figure 1C shows the pressure-volume curve with end-expiratory lung volume (EELV) values for two individuals (1 and 2).
Lung volumes of mild, moderate, and severe COPD patients were studied at rest, at 1/3 maximal power output (Wmax), and at 2/3 Wmax (Figure 2). Graphs T, E, Z do not necessarily correspond to mild, moderate, and severe states in this order.
Figure 1. A ERV - expiratory reserve volume; FRC - functional residual capacity; IC - inspiratory capacity; IRV - inspiratory reserve volume; RV - residual volume; TLC - total lung capacity; VC - vital capacity; VT - tidal volume. B Lung volume changes in mild (L), moderate (M), and severe (S) COPD patients. C Pressure-volume curve with end-expiratory lung volume (EELV) for two individuals (1 and 2).
Figure 2. End-expiratory and end-inspiratory volumes at rest (R), 1/3 Wmax, and 2/3 Wmax. Y - volume % of TLC. Panels T, E, and Z represent three COPD severity groups, not necessarily in mild/moderate/severe order.
On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.
A. Inspiratory muscles of person 1 generate lower force than person 2.TRUEFALSEB. In severe COPD compared to moderate, TLC does not increase, only the volume proportions of it change.TRUEFALSEC. In Figure 2, panel T corresponds to mild, Z to moderate, and E to severe cases of COPDTRUEFALSED. According to Figure 1C, person 2 has higher RV than person 1.TRUEFALSECheck AnswersTry Again← Previous: Q44Next: Q46 →Question reproduced from IBO 2024, Theoretical Exam Part B, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 - attributed to the International Biology Olympiad. data:
Theoretical BReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseComparative Osmoregulation & ExcretionEchiniscoides sigismundi, a marine tardigrade, can change its activity level and morphology when exposed to osmotic and chemical stress. To study this, a series of experiments with different environmental conditions was conducted, and the tardigrades’ activity levels were measured. Each experiment consisted of three time periods (24 hours each) during which the environmental changes were applied (Figure 1, panels A–H).
Osmotic conditions used: ultrapure water (~0‰), saturated seawater (~240‰), and natural habitat seawater (Lsw). Chemicals used: DNP - a mitochondrial uncoupling agent. In some cases osmotic and chemical conditions were applied together (e.g. DNP(~240‰) means DNP + saturated seawater).
Figure 1 (panels A–D). X - time (h), Y - activity (%). Panel A: natural seawater (Lsw) throughout. Panel B: ~0‰ (ultrapure water) from 0–24h, then Lsw. Panel C: ~240‰ (saturated seawater) from 0–24h, then Lsw. Panel D: DNP(Lsw) from 0–24h, then Lsw. All activity levels at t = 72h in panels B, C, D are not significantly different from panel A.
Figure 1 (panels E–H, continued). X - time (h), Y - activity (%). Panel E: DNP(~0‰) from 0–24h, then Lsw. Panel F: DNP(~240‰) from 0–24h, then Lsw. Panel G: DNP(Lsw) from 0–24h, then ~240‰, then Lsw. Panel H: ~240‰ from 0–24h, then DNP(Lsw), then Lsw. “” - significantly different, “ns” - not significantly different from the corresponding graphs (B, C, D) at t = 72h.*
On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.
A. Chemical stress has a more pronounced impact on activity level compared to osmotic one.TRUEFALSEB. ATP is crucial to tolerate hypoosmotic environments.TRUEFALSEC. It is evident that DNP followed by either hypoosmotic or hyperosmotic conditions has the same impact on activity level at t=72h.TRUEFALSED. DNP exposure without osmotic stress is sufficient for a marine tardigrade's morphological changes to happenTRUEFALSECheck AnswersTry Again← Previous: Q45Next: Q47 →Question reproduced from IBO 2024, Theoretical Exam Part B, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 - attributed to the International Biology Olympiad. data:
Theoretical BReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseImmune PhysiologyCancer immunotherapy is a cancer treatment approach where the body’s immune cells attack tumor cells. During their development, tumor cells accumulate many neoantigens (new antigens) - the more neoantigens present on the cell surface of tumor cells, the more efficiently immune cells destroy them. An “immune checkpoint” is the primary interaction between an immune cell and a tumor cell, in which the immune cell “decides” whether to attack the tumor cell or not.
However, tumor cells can avoid immune surveillance by hijacking the physiological pathway controlling T-cell activity (Figure 1A). To prevent tumor cells from escaping immune attack, checkpoint inhibitors have been developed (Figure 1A).
Figure 1. A The interaction between tumor and immune cells. B The serum of two cancer patients (R and Z) was applied to fixed human epithelial cells from a healthy donor; cells were then washed and stained with fluorescently labeled secondary antibodies against human immunoglobulins and visualized by fluorescence microscopy (immunotherapy should be avoided for one of these two patients). C Clinical results of checkpoint-inhibitor treatment on two cancer patient cohorts; the only significant difference between cohorts is the deficiency or proficiency of DNA mismatch repair.
On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.
A. Based on Figure 1, the main purpose of checkpoint inhibitors is to generate antibodies against tumor cells.TRUEFALSEB. An antibody against PDL-1 of cancer cells can be a successful strategy in immunotherapy.TRUEFALSEC. An oncologist is more likely to prescribe immunotherapy to Patient Z than to Patient R.TRUEFALSED. Most likely, cohort B has DNA mismatch repair-deficient tumors.TRUEFALSECheck AnswersTry Again← Previous: Q46Next: Q48 →Question reproduced from IBO 2024, Theoretical Exam Part B, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 - attributed to the International Biology Olympiad. data:
Theoretical BReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseImmune PhysiologyAn mRNA vaccine is a type of vaccine where a pathogenic antigen is encoded in an mRNA sequence. Upon delivery to the human body, cells translate this mRNA and make protein antigens - examples of mRNA vaccines include vaccines developed against the SARS-CoV-2 virus.
Before the development of mRNA vaccines, various forms of RNA nucleotide modifications had been tested for the immunogenic potential of mRNA itself (Figure 1). Note that under normal physiological conditions, RNA can exist outside cells in body fluids.
Figure 1. A Activatory response of antigen-presenting dendritic cells to specific RNA nucleotide modifications, recorded as cell-surface receptor levels (UN: unmodified). Each dot represents a single dendritic cell; above the threshold, dendritic cells are activated, expressing higher levels of both CD83 and MHC-II. B Efficiency of modified mRNAs’ translation by cells (UN: unmodified).
On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.
A. It is expected that the body's mRNA is modified to prevent auto-immune response.TRUEFALSEB. mRNA vaccines having s2U modifications will have the highest efficiency in generating viral antigens.TRUEFALSEC. mRNA vaccines against SARS-CoV-2 are more likely to contain m5C than pseudouridine (Ψ).TRUEFALSED. Both leukocytes and erythrocytes can serve as a host to produce antigens encoded in mRNA vaccines.TRUEFALSECheck AnswersTry Again← Previous: Q47Next: Q49 →Question reproduced from IBO 2024, Theoretical Exam Part B, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 - attributed to the International Biology Olympiad. Theoretical BReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseNervous System PhysiologyIn fruit flies, dietary content affects arousal to mechanical vibrations during sleep, a process mediated by enteroendocrine cells in the gut (Figure 1).
Figure 1. A The interaction scheme between enteroendocrine (EE) cells (secreting CCHa1) and the central nervous system. B The effect of dietary content on CCHa1 expression (Y-1: CCHa1 mRNA level in the gut; A: regular food, B: +sugar [14 kcal], C: +fat [80 kcal], D: +protein [40 kcal]). C The effect of CCHa1 depletion on arousal during sleep (Y-2: % flies awoken by stimulation). D The impact of the shi-ts mutation (defective endocytosis/exocytosis in the DA neuron) on arousal during sleep. E The impact of overexpressing TrpA1 (a cation channel transporting Na⁺ and Ca²⁺) in MBON neurons on arousal during sleep; Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ concentrations are lower inside the neuron than outside.
On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.
A. CCHa1 expression depends on the caloric content of the consumed food.TRUEFALSEB. Results suggest that a protein-rich diet reduces sleep arousal.TRUEFALSEC. CCHa1 should result in the excitation of DA neurons to prevent arousal during sleep.TRUEFALSED. The synapse between DA and MBON neurons should be inhibitory to prevent arousal during sleep.TRUEFALSECheck AnswersTry Again← Previous: Q48Next: Q50 →Question reproduced from IBO 2024, Theoretical Exam Part B, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 - attributed to the International Biology Olympiad. data:
Theoretical BReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseBioenergetics & Central Metabolism OverviewKetogenic (high-fat, low-carbohydrate) diet is an efficient treatment for recurrent seizures, as in epilepsy. Ketogenic diet is thought to exert its effect via a metabolic pathway shown in Figure 1, as it leads to a production of beta-hydroxybutyrate. Increasing the number of reactions in a biochemical pathway decreases its overall reaction rate.
Figure 1. Glycolysis and ketolysis both feed into the TCA cycle via acetyl-CoA (reaction 1) and citrate (reaction 2); TCA-cycle intermediates alpha-ketoglutarate and oxaloacetate connect to the glutamate/GABA/aspartate shunt (reaction 3).
Dopamine is known to play a role in muscle control (e.g., its deficiency is one of the causes of Parkinson’s disease). A study investigated the interaction of catecholamines (dopamine, noradrenaline, and adrenaline) with a ketogenic diet. The study used Dbh knockout (Dbh-/-) and heterozygote (Dbh+/-) mice that were fed with either a ketogenic or normal diet. To estimate the efficacy of the diet in each group, they were introduced to fluorothyl (a seizure-inducing agent), and the latency to the first seizure was measured.
Figure 2. A Metabolism of catecholamines. B Seizure latency threshold (in milliseconds) after provocation with fluorothyl in Dbh +/- and -/- mice fed either the standard or ketogenic diet. Asterisk indicates a significant difference.
On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.
A. A ketogenic diet facilitates the conversion of alpha-ketoglutarate to glutamate.TRUEFALSEB. A mutation reducing the Km of the enzyme that catalyzes reaction 2 in Figure 1 decreases the value of the seizure latency (in milliseconds) in (Dbh+/-) mice with a ketogenic diet.TRUEFALSEC. L-DOPA can be used as both an anti-convulsant and a treatment for Parkinson's disease.TRUEFALSED. The study is certainly conclusive that noradrenaline enhances GABA's anti-seizure functions.TRUEFALSECheck AnswersTry Again← Previous: Q4Next: Q6 →Question reproduced from IBO 2024, Theoretical Exam Part B, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 - attributed to the International Biology Olympiad. data:
Theoretical BReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseEvolutionary Developmental Biology (Evo-Devo)During Drosophila development, oogenesis establishes the body plan before fertilization.
The concentration gradient of bicoid mRNA in the oocyte determines the anterior-posterior axis (Figure 1A), a process controlled by the Exuperantia protein. Exuperantia anchors bicoid mRNA at the anterior end of the oocyte, preventing its free diffusion and thereby shaping the distribution of bicoid protein in the developing embryo (Figure 1B).
The concentration gradient of the gurken protein (Figure 1C) and its positive interaction with the torpedo protein is critical for determining the dorsoventral axis of the embryo. Interestingly, a wild-type oocyte inside a torpedo-deficient follicle develops into an entirely ventral embryo, while a torpedo-deficient oocyte inside a wild-type follicle develops a normal body plan.
Figure 1. A Y-1: bicoid mRNA concentration; Ant: anterior, Pos: posterior. B Y-2: bicoid protein concentration; Ac: acron, H: head, Th: thorax, Ab: abdomen, Te: telson. C O: oocyte, FC: follicle cells, G: concentration gradient of gurken.
On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.
A. You can deplete bicoid in male testes to get mutant embryos lacking head and thorax regions.TRUEFALSEB. An Exuperantia loss-of-function mutant embryo will have an extended acron.TRUEFALSEC. Torpedo gene expression is not required in oocytes for establishing the normal dorsal-ventral axis.TRUEFALSED. The arrow in Figure 1C points from the dorsal to the ventral part of the future embryo.TRUEFALSECheck AnswersTry Again← Previous: Q49Back to Theoretical B →Question reproduced from IBO 2024, Theoretical Exam Part B, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 - attributed to the International Biology Olympiad. data:
Theoretical BReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseRecombinant DNA & Biotechnology TechniquesProQC is a synthetic biology tool used for the quality control of protein expression. ProQC consists of a synthetic gene-expression complex that only allows the expression of gene of interest (GOI)-encoded protein only from the full-length mRNAs. It is composed of two parts: a toehold switch containing a ribosome binding site (RBS) at the 5’ end of the GOI, and a cis-trigger at the 3’ end of the GOI, both under the same promoter. The sequence of the cis-trigger is reverse complementary to the toehold switch. When the toehold switch portion of the synthetic cassette is free, it forms a hairpin-like structure that blocks the RBS sequence.
Figure 1. Schematic diagram of one of the possible conformations of the ProQC system.
On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.
A. The ProQC system allows translation only when the cis-trigger binds to the toehold switch.TRUEFALSEB. The ProQC system increases the yield of functional proteins and reduces the waste of cellular resources.TRUEFALSEC. This system is not necessary in eukaryotic cells.TRUEFALSED. In the ProQC system, the RBS in the toehold switch can be unblocked by trigger RNA transcribed separately from the ProQC system.TRUEFALSECheck AnswersTry Again← Previous: Q5Next: Q7 →Question reproduced from IBO 2024, Theoretical Exam Part B, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 - attributed to the International Biology Olympiad. data:
Theoretical BReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseDNA Structure & ReplicationDNA fiber assay is used to study various aspects of DNA synthesis, such as replication speed, replication origin firing, and replication termination. It utilizes modified nucleotides to visualize the progression of DNA replication directly. In this assay, cellular DNA is sequentially labeled with chloro-deoxyuridine (CldU) followed by iodo-deoxyuridine (IdU), each for an equal period. Upon replication, cells incorporate these modified nucleotides into newly synthesized DNA. Next, cells are lysed and individual DNA fibers are stretched on a microscopic slide, followed by CldU (red) and IdU (blue) antibody staining. Finally, DNA fibers are visualized by fluorescent microscopy.
Figure 1. Panels A-F represent replicated DNA segments. Each panel shows a single uninterrupted DNA molecule labeled with CldU (red) followed by IdU (blue). The white bar at the bottom right of each panel is a scale bar of 10 μm. The DNA in all panels is from the same organism.
On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.
A. Panel A can represent replication progression from a single replication fork, while panel B shows replication progression from two forks.TRUEFALSEB. Both panels C and E demonstrate replication termination.TRUEFALSEC. In panel B, CldU is incorporated into either a leading or lagging strand of DNA but not into both.TRUEFALSED. The DNA belongs to a bacterial species.TRUEFALSECheck AnswersTry Again← Previous: Q6Next: Q8 →Question reproduced from IBO 2024, Theoretical Exam Part B, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 - attributed to the International Biology Olympiad. Theoretical BReal exam question - full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licenseBiomolecular Analytical TechniquesAn in vitro experiment with enzymes involved in DNA metabolism was performed using the double-stranded DNA substrate shown in Figure 1. The upper strand of the DNA substrate is 50 bases, and the 5’ is labeled with blue fluorescent dye, while the lower strand is 100 bases, and the 3’ is labeled with red fluorescent dye. Fluorophore-labeled ends are chemically inert.
The reaction scheme is shown in Table 1. After each reaction, DNAs were separated using denaturing polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis to separate denatured single-stranded DNAs (Figure 2, the purple color indicates the presence of both DNA strands at the same position).
Figure 1 (substrate diagram) and Figure 2 (gel result), with Table 1 (reaction scheme): reaction 1 = DNA substrate alone; reaction 2 = + enzyme A; reaction 3 = + enzyme B; reaction 4 = + enzyme A, then inactivate A, then + enzyme C; reaction 5 = + enzyme B, then inactivate B, then + enzyme C.
On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.
A. Enzyme A is an endonuclease, generating blunt-ended breaks.TRUEFALSEB. Enzyme B is an exonuclease with a 3'-5' polarity.TRUEFALSEC. Enzyme C is a DNA polymerase.TRUEFALSED. If an additional reaction were performed with enzyme C alone, the result would be the same as the result of reaction 4.TRUEFALSECheck AnswersTry Again← Previous: Q7Next: Q9 →Question reproduced from IBO 2024, Theoretical Exam Part B, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 - attributed to the International Biology Olympiad. BiOGuide is a free, non-commercial study resource. Almost everything on the site - every topic page, every practice question, every timed attempt - works with no account at all. This page explains what happens on the small part that does involve an account: login, your profile, and the leaderboard.
data.a-note-for-younger-users#A note for youn: BiOGuide’s audience includes a lot of school-age students. If you’re under the age required in your country to agree to this kind of policy on your own (for example, under 13 in the US), please ask a parent or guardian to help you sign up, or to reach out to us at the email above with any questions or a deletion request on your behalf.
data.accounts-are-optional#Accounts are optio: You can read every topic page and attempt every practice question without ever signing up. An account only unlocks saving leaderboard results, a profile, and full access to BiOInsights.
data.changes-to-this-policy#Changes to this p: If this policy changes in any meaningful way, we’ll update the “Last updated” date at the top of this page. Since BiOGuide is run by one person rather than a legal team, treat this as a clear, honest first pass rather than a final legal document - if you have concerns, please just email us.
data.cookies-and-local-storage#Cookies and lo: We don’t use tracking or advertising cookies. Your login session is kept in your browser’s local storage (not a third-party cookie) so you stay logged in between visits - this is standard behavior for any site with accounts, not a tracking mechanism.
data.deleting-your-data#Deleting your data:
If you have an account, you can delete it yourself at any time: log in, go to the Account page, and use Delete my account at the bottom of your profile. This permanently and immediately removes your login, profile, avatar/country/education/about, and all leaderboard/attempt history - it cannot be undone. We keep a minimal internal record that a deletion occurred (just a date and an internal ID, nothing identifying) so we can confirm a deletion happened if you ever ask us to check.
If you’d rather we do it for you, or you have any other privacy question, email us at r6394175@gmail.com.
data.what-we-collect#What we collect:
If you never create an account, we don’t collect anything about you beyond standard, anonymous web hosting logs (handled by our host, Vercel).
If you create an account (optional, via Sign Up on the Account page), we collect:
Email and password - used only to log you in. Passwords are never stored in readable form; authentication is handled by our backend provider, Supabase, using industry-standard hashing. We never see or store your raw password. Display name - chosen at signup, shown publicly on the leaderboard. Avatar - a picture you pick from a small curated set, shown publicly next to your name. Country, education level, and a short “about” bio - all optional, filled in on your profile. Country is shown publicly on the leaderboard as a flag; education level and “about” are shown only on your own profile. Timed Attempt / quiz activity - if you submit a practice test to the leaderboard, we store your score, timing, and per-question results, tied to your account, so we can rank you and show your history. That’s the complete list. We don’t collect payment information (the site is free), and we don’t run third-party ad or tracking scripts.
data.where-its-stored#Where it\u0026rsquo;s s:
Account and profile data lives in Supabase, a hosted Postgres database and authentication provider. The site itself is hosted on Vercel. Both are reputable infrastructure providers used by many websites - naming them here is normal and doesn’t mean either can see or use your data beyond storing/serving it on our behalf.
Row-level security rules mean other logged-in users can never read your email or your private practice-test details directly from the database - only what’s meant to be public (display name, avatar, country, leaderboard results) is visible to others.
data.why-we-collect-it#Why we collect it: Only to run the features you’re actually using: logging you in, showing your chosen name/avatar/country on the leaderboard, and keeping a record of your practice-test results so the leaderboard and your own history stay accurate. We don’t sell data, and we don’t use it for advertising.

data.a-note-on-devices#A Note on Devices: This site is best used on a laptop, PC, or equivalent. During testing, a few features, the 3D graphs (Streamlit/Plotly) and the mock IBO 2022 practical, weren’t available on mobile. The written notes themselves are fully accessible on any device. Sorry for the inconvenience in the meantime.
data.books--graded-resources#Books \u0026amp;:
We’ve collected and graded the most useful books and resources in this Drive folder.
The grading (S/A/B) isn’t a strict ranking, S doesn’t automatically mean “better than” A or B. It reflects relevance and recommendation for a given purpose more than raw quality. If you’d like to help with grading resources, fill out this survey and we’ll be in touch.

data.how-this-guide-approaches-teaching#How T:
Biology olympiads test comprehensive logical reasoning rather than pure rote memorisation, but that’s a double-edged sword. Lean too heavily on working things out from the question context alone, without solid concept familiarity underneath, and your accuracy and your time management both suffer. So while you don’t need to memorise everything, genuine familiarity with the core concepts and ideas matters more here than in most exams.
This guide leans on interactive material, static diagrams, and dense text over video. That’s deliberate: we want you to build understanding through words and images/graphs first, since that’s closer to how you’ll actually need to reason during the exam. Most students using this guide aren’t aiming for the international stage or a research career either, so the notes are written to be useful at every level of Biology Olympiad preparation, not just for students chasing IBO qualification.
For material this guide doesn’t cover in enough depth, the USABO Handouts are a good beginner-friendly supplement (though a little thin for more advanced students).

This unit covers the biological foundations that the rest of the syllabus builds on: how cells are organised and communicate, how the genome is stored, copied, read, and regulated, and the core chemistry of the molecules that make all of it possible. It presumes basic high-school chemistry and mathematics; if you want to firm up the basics first, these handouts are a good starting point: Biochemistry Handout, Part 1, Part 2.
The section is organised in three tiers: Cell Biology (how cells are structured and organised), Molecular Biology (how the genome is stored, copied, and expressed), and Biochemistry (the chemistry underlying it all). Start with Cell Theory below if you’re new to the subject: everything else builds on it.
1. Cell Theory, Prokaryotes & EukaryotesThe three tenets of cell theory and the structural/genomic distinctions between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, read this first.
